title: The Gopis Grieve at His Leaving
story:
Krishna had grown up in the cowherd village of Vrindavan, in the house of Nanda, the chief of the cowherds; and the gopis — the cowherd women of the village — loved him as the light of their days. So when Nanda gave the word, it fell on them like a blow. Gather all the milk and its products, he told the men; tomorrow we go to Mathura, and we will carry the king his tribute. For Akrura, the king's messenger, had come to carry Krishna away with him — and no one could say when the village would see him again.

Some of the gopis lost the light from their faces, their breath coming short. Others stopped in the middle of their work, lost in the thought of him. Still others stood remembering his smiles, his way of walking, his laughing glances, the softness of his look — and trembled at the separation that was coming. They turned on Akrura.

You showed us his face, they said, framed by those dark curls — the fair cheeks, the fine nose, the little smile that chases away every sorrow — and now you are doing us a cruel wrong, carrying him out of our sight. You are called Akrura, "not cruel," and yet you are cruel indeed: you gave us these eyes, and now you steal away the very thing they were given to see.

Others thought of the city, and their fear sharpened. The night will pass pleasantly for the women of Mathura, they said; their wishes have come true. Tomorrow the eyes of the whole city will feast on him, and we will be left here with nothing. He will hear their sweet, polished speech, and he will never again endure our rustic words. He won our hearts with words sweeter than honey, and now he will wander off, charmed by the bashful smiles of those simple city women. Nanda's son is new to affection; his friendship can break in a moment. We gave up our homes, our kin, our children, our husbands to serve him — and now, how will he ever look at us again?

Let us go and stop Krishna, one of them said. What can our elders and kinsmen do to us now? There stands Akrura, the dry-hearted one, already seated on his chariot, and the proud ones are urging him to hurry.

And they remembered the evenings, which were the hardest of all to remember. At the close of day Krishna used to come back into the village with the cowherds around him — the dust of hooves on his hair and garland, playing his flute, casting his smiling, sidelong glances — and he would steal their hearts all over again. His sweet words, his playful looks, his embraces had made their nights pass like a single moment. Without him, they asked one another, how were we ever to cross the darkness that stretched ahead?

They wept, their bracelets hanging loose upon arms grown thin with sorrow, and the thought of his going lay on the whole village through the night.
reflection: The gopis' grief is remarkable for how precise it is. They name exactly what they will lose — his face, his smile, his flute at evening, the dust of hooves on his hair — and they fear, with reason, that the polished city will outbid their rustic love. Their sorrow is not vague; it is a catalogue of a life.
next_story_tease: But Krishna would not leave them to their weeping without a word.
hero_scene: A cluster of gopis grieving in Vrindavan as word of the journey spreads, one pressing a hand to her heart while others look toward the road to Mathura, Akrura's chariot and the loaded carts in the background.
